findings.claim: Gap 3's rationale gives a false lexical ground for excluding 'dismissive': brevity CAN be dismissive, so the block is contextual irrelevance, not a selectional/sense violation.
findings.evidence: Rationale q3: "dismissive = sense misfit; it describes an attitude a person takes, and brevity is a property of a document, not a stance." But 'dismissive brevity' / 'his brevity was not dismissive' are ordinary English — brevity is routinely predicated as dismissive. The same rationale gets the parallel case right one clause later: "excessive = sense misfit; 'excessive brevity' is ordinary English (too terse), so the block is not grammar but relevance."
findings.why: The rationale is the teaching payload; a student who has met 'dismissive brevity' will see the stated reason is wrong and lose trust in the explanation. Does not change the key ('far from dismissive' says nothing about whether shortening helped, so D 'decisive' remains the single best), hence minor rather than verdict-changing — but it is exactly the class of false rationale claim the pedagogy stage exists to catch, and MINOR_FIXES already touched this sentence's neighbour.

findings.claim: Gap 2's rationale mis-describes the option set as one connective class; 'Naturally' is a stance/attitudinal disjunct, not a conjunct like the three distractors, making the key the odd one out by adverb class.
findings.evidence: Rationale q2: "Connective gap; four sentence-initial adverbs of the same connective class." Options are Naturally / Consequently / Conversely / Ultimately. 'Consequently', 'Conversely' and 'Ultimately' are linking adverbials (result, contrast, summative); 'Naturally' is a content disjunct meaning 'as one would expect' — the rationale itself glosses it that way ("'Naturally' ('as one would expect')"), i.e. not as a connective relation at all.
findings.why: Two consequences: (a) a stated fact in the teaching payload is inaccurate; (b) a test-wise student can reach the key by 'pick the one that is not a logical connector' without reading the paragraph. The cue is faint — it requires knowing adverb subclasses, which is close to the construct being measured — and M-TELL and G-DISTRACTOR both passed on the set, so this is a note rather than a refutation.

findings.claim: Gap 1's rationale re-quotes the passage frame inconsistently: the substitution illustration silently drops 'just', which is present in the verbatim frame quoted earlier in the same rationale.
findings.evidence: Passage: "few of her volunteers could give any ___(1)___ of what they had just agreed to". Rationale q1 first quotes it correctly ("'few of her volunteers could give any ___ of what they had just agreed to'"), then writes "'give any discount of what they had agreed to' collapses into nonsense" — 'just' removed. Mechanical check against the passage: the first string matches verbatim, the second returns MISS.
findings.why: The integrated stage's own rule is that quoted phrases must be verbatim against current text. Here it is a constructed substitution rather than a citation, so nothing is factually wrong, but the same rationale quotes the same frame two ways — the sort of drift the integrated read is meant to normalise.

findings.claim: Gap 3's rationale attributes to text 'that follows' a figure that precedes the gap.
findings.evidence: Rationale q3: "The evidence that follows — shortening the terms to a single page moved the median from eleven seconds to twenty-two ...". The eleven-second median is stated in paragraph 1 ("the median time spent on the terms and conditions was eleven seconds"), before gap (3); only the rise ("the median rose — to twenty-two seconds") follows it.
findings.why: The inference is sound and the arithmetic reconciles, but the locator is wrong, and locators matter in a cloze rationale that is teaching students where to look ('read two sentences past the gap' is the family's own sample technique).

findings.claim: No further language defect found; the CORRECTED verdict is substantiated by the specific repair in the diff, and the repair is clean.
findings.evidence: G-ENG-2 flagged "'quietly' recurs two sentences later ('has quietly stopped asking')"; candidates -> candidates-corrected changes that clause to "has long since stopped asking", leaving 'quietly' once. Spelling variety holds BrE throughout ('behaviour', 'signed up to', 'on offer'; no AmE-only forms in passage or any of the 20 options). Number style spelled out consistently ('a hundred', 'eleven', 'nine thousand', 'twenty-two'). Subject-verb agreement checked at the one long subject ('the median time spent on the terms and conditions was eleven seconds'). Spaced em dashes used consistently. Remaining repeated content words (Hallenbeck x4, volunteers x3, enough x3, choice/strike/decision x2) are all deliberate rhetorical parallels, not editorial slips.
findings.why: Recorded for completeness of the adversarial pass: I attempted and failed to refute the language stage.
